name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox

lead: A screen curfew stops phone, computer and TV use some time before bed; a dopamine detox goes further and temporarily abstains from stimulating activities. People in looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities use both to sleep earlier and better, which feeds into skin, less puffiness, energy and focus.

Reference sources describe evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs as able to delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality, which supports the curfew. Dopamine fasting was popularized by psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it targets impulsive behaviors rather than literally lowering dopamine; neuroscientists have criticized the name and the idea of a brain reset. There is no defined protocol or trials for the detox.

paras: People put devices away an hour or more before bed and charge them outside the bedroom. Dopamine detox versions set aside hours or days without social media, games or other high-stimulation activity.
No direct harms are documented for a curfew. Extreme versions of dopamine fasting, such as avoiding food or social contact, have been criticized by clinicians.

angle.text: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation helps you fall asleep earlier and sleep better, which shows in skin, puffiness and energy. The evening-light logic has research behind it; the dopamine framing is disputed by neuroscientists.

lead: A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities such as scrolling, gaming and snacking. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are used to get better sleep and focus, and to free time for training, skincare and other habits that change how a person looks.

The appearance chain runs through sleep. Evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs can delay circadian timing and reduce sleep quality.[1] In an experimental BMJ study, people photographed after sleep restriction were rated less healthy and less attractive than after a normal night, and later work measured changes in skin colour, eye openness, mouth curvature and periorbital darkness after sleep deprivation.[2][3][4]

Dopamine fasting was popularised by California psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it is a cognitive behavioural technique targeting impulsive behaviours rather than a literal lowering of dopamine; neuroscientists have criticised the name and the idea of a brain "reset".[5]
infobox: No phone before bed; breaks from social media, gaming, snacking

paras: The practice rests on research on evening light, which can delay circadian timing and suppress melatonin, with blue-rich device light cited as most potent.[1] General sleep-hygiene guidance recommends avoiding bright light before bed, although overall evidence that sleep hygiene alone improves insomnia is weak, according to a 2021 meta-analysis cited in Wikipedia's sleep hygiene article.[6]

Dopamine fasting has no fixed definition: some versions restrict only online technology, others also restrict food, work, exercise or conversation, and targets include social media, gaming, shopping, emotional eating and pornography.[5] Sepah has said the goal is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not dopamine itself.[5] Critics, including neuroscientist Ciara McCabe, call the idea of resetting the brain scientifically unfounded; physician Peter Grinspoon described Sepah's underlying approach as sensible while cautioning against extreme versions.[5]
Wikipedia notes that a study of adults aged 30 to 45 found more screen time linked to higher impulsivity, and that freeing time from poor habits may allow healthier activities such as exercise.[5]

On looksmax.org, threads promote dopamine detoxes as a way to escape constant stimulation from scrolling, rapid content and notifications and to become more productive.[7] Other users report mixed results; one thread describes cutting social media, music and most device time for a week, using a greyscale phone, and still finding everything bland.[8] Hacker News posted several videos on the topic in 2023.[9][9]

No studies found of dopamine fasting or a formal screen curfew as defined in these communities. Related research covers evening light exposure and sleep,[1] sleep hygiene as a general category with inconclusive results,[6] and how restricted sleep changes facial appearance.[2][3][4]

lore.intro: Dopamine detox appears on looksmax.org as a discipline and productivity practice, with accounts both enthusiastic and underwhelmed.[7][8]

claims.claim: Constant scrolling overstimulates the brain, and a detox resets focus.
